title: Santa Claus Conquers the Martians

evidence.note: Renewal absence cannot make this 1964 film public domain. For a work first published in 1964, 17 U.S.C. 304(a) provides a renewal term whether or not a renewal application is filed (304(a)(3)(B): an application 'is not a condition of the renewal and extension'), so the queue's 'renewal_absent_likely' premise does not apply. Public domain would have to rest on a missing copyright notice on the 1964 release prints, and I could not verify that from any source I fetched. Secondary sources (Plagiarism Today, Wikipedia) say the film is public domain in the US but do not document the basis.
Sound film. The recorded soundtrack normally shares the film's status, so it is undetermined for the same reason as the print. I did not verify any separate music copyright or registration.

Wikipedia and a web search both credit the screenplay to Paul L. Jacobson, based on a story by Glenville Mareth. I did not confirm whether the story was published or registered separately, so the story layer is undetermined.

Plagiarism Today and Wikipedia say that outside the US, STUDIOCANAL holds the copyright and enforces it. I did not confirm a specific restoration or its added material. Any cleaned-up transfer, new titles or added commentary would be protectable even if the underlying print were free.

renewal_search.negative_result: Not run. Renewal is not the controlling question for a 1964 work under 17 U.S.C. 304(a), so a renewal-absence search would not establish public domain status here.

editorial:
Santa Claus Conquers the Martians is a 1964 children's science-fiction comedy directed by Nicholas Webster. Paul L. Jacobson wrote and produced it through Jalor Productions, from a story credited to Glenville Mareth, and Embassy Pictures distributed it, premiering it on November 14, 1964. Martian children have stopped playing because they watch Earth television, so their leader abducts Santa Claus. The film was a staple of local TV, appeared on Mystery Science Theater 3000 in 1991, and is widely shared as a public-domain holiday title.

The rights trap is the usual shortcut, that an old film was never renewed. A film published in 1964 got its renewal term automatically under 17 U.S.C. 304(a), so renewal is not what decides this one. It would have to lapse for another reason, such as a missing notice, and I found no document establishing that. Secondary sources call it public domain in the US only, and say STUDIOCANAL still holds and enforces rights abroad. Check the notice on an actual print before reusing it, and keep it out of non-US distribution.
faq: Is Santa Claus Conquers the Martians public domain because the copyright was not renewed?

That reason does not work for a 1964 film. Under 17 U.S.C. 304(a) the renewal term attaches automatically, and filing a renewal application is not a condition of it. The film could be public domain in the US only through a defect such as a missing copyright notice. I could not verify one, so the status is undetermined here.
Can I use the Internet Archive copies, including outside the US?

The Internet Archive copies are community uploads, and I have not verified the source or quality of either. Plagiarism Today reports that outside the US, STUDIOCANAL holds and enforces the copyright. For anything beyond US use, get a clearance first.
